full_judgment:
2. The Additional Deputy Commissioner Dacca, assessed compensation for the acquired land, but owner-Respondents were not satisfied with the assessment. They moved the Court under the Land Acquisition Act, since no tribunal under the Act was set up to determine the compensation. The Additional District Judge as the Court by its order dated 21.5.66 awarded for various items claimed by the owner a sum of Taka 1,17,117/74 together with 6% interest from the date of the award. 

 6. The all important question in this appeal is the first question. It is to be remembered that the award was given by the Court under the Land Acquisition Act in terms of S. 91A of the Act, since no tribunal was constituted under the Act. The learned Attorney-General has submitted that the view taken by the High Court that appeal does not lie from an award made under S. 93A of the Town Improvement Act, but revision lies is not sustainable. He submits that if the appeal does not lie in terms of sub-section (6) of S. 93A, then revision equally is incompetent because it will be an award of the tribunal and not a court subordinate to the High Court in terms of S. 115, Civil Procedure Code. He has further elaborated his argument by reference to various provisions of the Town Improvement Act and the Land Acquisition Act. He says, in support of his contention that in the present case no tribunal has been constituted under the Act, either to arbitrate or adjudicate the disputed compensation payable for the properties acquired under S. 93A. He further says, S. 91A provides in such contingency determination of compensation by the Court under the Land Acquisition Act. He says, the Act except for mentioning the Court under the Land Acquisition Act, has not provided for any trial procedure, or the character of the award or its enforcement, or appeal therefrom. The two enactments, are in pari materia and should be read together as one enactment, applying the principle of generalia specialibus non deregant. According to him, applying this maxim, we get that in terms of S. 54 of the Land Acquisition Act the award is appealable to the High Court. 

 7. The question requires some investigation. It is to be remembered that in the original scheme of the Act, S. 93A was not there. It was first introduced in 1958 by East Pakistan Ordinance LXIX of 1958, and thereafter has undergone various amendments from time to time. Introduction of this section, it appears, was prompted by the desire to introduce measures for requisition and acquisition of property under this Act as well. An attempt was made to make this section self-contained but on scrutiny, it seems, that the attempt has not achieved the desired result, and the learned Attorney-General's submission in this regard is justified. This fact has caused the complexity to the question. 

 8. The parent section contains seven sub-sections and several clauses and has provided for requisition, and has provided for requisition property. Sub-sect (5) provides the manner, method and forum of assessment of compensation. This sub-section requires some consideration. Clause (a) says, compensation of property requisitioned or acquired under S. 93A shall be fixed by agreement; sub-clause (i) to clause (b) says, when no such agreement can be reached the Deputy Commissioner shall assess compensation with reference to those provisions of the Land Acquisition Act as are mentioned and modified by this Act. Sub-clause (ii) to clause (b) says, within the prescribed time as given in proviso to sub-clause (iii), any person interested, who has not accepted the assessment made by the Deputy Commissioner, may move the Tribunal to determine the matter; sub-clause (c) says, at the commencement of the proceeding the respective parties shall state their opinion what the fair compensation is. Sub-section (6) says, sections 88 and 91 of Act providing appeal shall not apply to property requisitioned or acquired under this section. 

 10. The Town Improvement Act, however, has not kept the problem in vacuum and such contingency is met by S. 91A. The section says, among others, if the Provincial Government does not constitute Tribunal in terms of S. 80, reference to Tribunal in S. 93A "shall be construed as referring to Court under Land Acquisition Act, 1894". A glance at the Act indicates that this Act does not intend to exclude the function of court under the Land Acquisition Act, if no tribunal is set up under Ss. 80 and 83. On the constitution of the Tribunal, diverse provisions of Act providing detailed procedure of diverse proceedings for acquisition of property for different purposes are attracted. Their consideration need not detain us, because in the present case the award was made not by the tribunal set up under the Act, but by the court under Land Acquisition Act in terms of S. 91A. 

 11. The crucial point for consideration, is, what upon the true construction is the meaning of the expression, "shall be construed as referring to the court under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894" in Sec. 91A. One way of interpreting it is to treat the court in this section to mean tribunal under the Town Improvement Act, if the language of the section could be so construed. Do we get any such language in this section? We find none. We cannot apply the restrictive provisions of the Act to the proceeding or award of the said Court by treating it a tribunal under the Act. The expression "shall be construed as referring to" is the well-known language employed by the Legislature in order to attract the provisions of an analogous enactment into the Act without enacting them over again. We may call the device, the scissors and paste method. This explains the purpose. 

 12. A comparative reading of the two enactments reveals, that they are in part materia. Town Improvement Act while providing for the method of assessment of compensation has liberally borrowed substantial provisions of the Land Acquisition Act. The Legislative Authority, in our opinion, has employed the language to incorporate substantial provisions of the Land Acquisition Act into this enactment. Scissors and paste method has been applied. The two enactments again are in part materia. The recognised rule of interpretation is to treat the two enactments as one system and explanatory to each other, subject to the further rule of 'generalia specialibus nondergant'. We are therefore to treat the two enactments as one and where there are overlapping provisions, the special or particular will exclude the general. We find that the Town Improvement Act provides for acquisition of land for Dacca and Narayanganj and certain areas in their vicinity. It is a special enactment. Land Acquisition Act on the other hand, provides for acquisition of land all over the country without any qualification. It is the general enactment on the subject of land acquisition. The rule of interpretation in such case is that the provision of the special law will prevail over the general law with which the former is inconsistent. Applying the rule of interpretation set out above, we find that for the lands acquired under the Town Improvement Act, its provisions shall apply, but for cases where the enactment is silent and there is no inconsistency between the two, the general law provided in Land Acquisition Act will apply to supplement the first. 

 13. To proceed, we find that S. 91A has, by necessary implication provided for the application of the relevant provisions of the Court under the L and Acquisition Act. Provisions of the Land Acquisition Act as to procedure, character of the award, its enforcement, and appeal therefore are attracted and shall apply, subject to any special provision applicable under Town Improvement Act. The latter Act has made provisions relating to the Tribunal set up under it. Sub-section (6) of section 93A has in clear language barred appeal from the award of the Tribunal set up under the Act. We are therefore again put back to the question whether the Court under the L and Acquisition Act shall be treated as Tribunal under the Town Improvement Act. Language of the enactment does not say so. No language has been employed in S. 91A which lends support to the reading of Tribunal substituting the Court. 

 14. Apart from the language of section 91A, if we look at the provision of S. 93A, we find, as already observed, that the attempt to make the section self contained has failed. To illustrate, the Tribunal mentioned in sub-clause (ii) or clause (b) of sub-section (5), we find., no trial procedure has been made, nothing has been said as to the character of the award made by the Tribunal, nor any provision for enforcement of the award, except that the award is not appealable as provided in sub-section (6). This total lack of provision to govern the Court under the Land Acquisition Act in terms of S. 91A, is a manifest indication of the legislative intent not to whittle down in any manner the power and jurisdiction the said court. A comparative reading of two enactments indicates that it is not possible either to read or to treat the Court under the Land Acquisition Act referred to in S. 91A as a tribunal under the Town Improvement Act. A contrary interpretation will lead to procedural vacuum and it should be avoided. In this view; the provisions of power, procedure, jurisdiction and appeal of the Land Acquisition Act shall apply in such cases. Under S. 54 of the Land Acquisition Act, the award is appealable to the High Court. For the reason we reverse conclusion of the High Court that no appeal lay from the award in the instant case. 

 16. Sub-section (5) of section 93A in plain language says, whenever any immovable property is requisitioned or acquired compensation shall be paid for it. Requisition is temporary deprivation of possession, whereas acquisition is permanent deprivation of both possession and title. Loss in the first case to the owner is temporary and partial, whereas in the latter it is total, but he suffers loss in either case to the extent of rent payable under the said Ordinance. Finding this difficulty, the learned Attorney-General did not press the point further. 

 17. As regards the first limb, it is clear that under second paragraph of sub-section (1) of S. 23, Land Acquisition Act made applicable by Town Improvement Act, does provide compensation for trees and the learned Attorney-General is well founded in saying that there is no provision in the Act for capitalisation of twenty years alleged profit to assess compensation for trees. He however conceded that the land owner is entitled to a reasonable compensation. Mr. Panday for the Respondents has failed to satisfy us that there is any provision or basis for such capitalisation. 

 18. The rule set out above only says, the owner is entitled to damages for trees on the land in acquisition. But there is no provision how the damages are to be assessed. The assessment of damages has therefore been left to the discretion of the authority or Court, and this discretion it is to be exercised reasonably and fairly. The reasonable compensation for a tree will therefore be its market value at the relevant time, and that will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The rule of twenty years capitalisation of the profit is arbitrary and artificial and not sanctioned by law. For the reason the decisions of the courts below on the assessment of compensation of trees cannot be sustained. 

 21. In my opinion, assessment of compensation made by the Land Acquisition Court under section 93A of the Town Improvement Act is not appealable, and the Bench of the Dacca High Court was correct in holding that the appeal preferred to it was incompetent. But at the same time I am also of the view that the High Court was not correct in holding that in the absence of any provision for appeal the High Court was competent to exercise its revisional jurisdiction in respect of such assessment, inasmuch as the Land Acquisition Court acting under section 93A of the Town Improvement Act did not function as a Court subordinate to the High Court within the meaning of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as was correctly contended by the learned Attorney-General in the alternative. 

 23. It has been argued by the learned Attorney-General that though there is no specific provision in the Town Improvement Act for appeal against an order of the Land Acquisition. Court determining compensation for the properties acquired under section 93A of the Town Improvement Act, the provision of appeal as contained in section 54 of the Land Acquisition Act will be attracted in respect of such determination by the Land Acquisition Court. It has been contended by the learned Counsel that when an assessment of compensation is made by the Land Acquisition Court in the absence of a Tribunal constituted under section 80 of the Town Improvement Act, all the pro-visions relating to such assessment as contained in the Land Acquisition Act including the provision for appeal will be applicable in respect of such assessment. The contention of the learned Attorney-General is virtually to the effect that although there is no provision for appeal in section 93A of the Town Improvement Act in respect of an order of assessment made by the Land Acquisition Court under the said section, but the right of appeal in respect of such an order is necessarily implied from the existence of such a right under the provision of Land Acquisition Act under which such a Court ordinarily functions. 

 25. The question whether there is a right of appeal against an order of assessment of compensation made by the Land Acquisition Court under section 93A of the Town Improvement Act, which purports to be a complete Code in itself, inevitably leads to a search for the legislative intent in respect of such a right, which is to be gathered from the provisions of the entire Act. It is now well established that a right of appeal is a substantive right which can be created by an express provision of a statute and cannot be deduced inferentially. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council had to consider a similar question in the case of Rangoon Botatoung Company Ltd. Vs. The Collector of Rangoon, reported in 39 I.A. 197 same case ILR 40 Cal. 21 BC in which a right of appeal to his Majesty in Council from a decision of the Court on reference under the Land Acquisition Act (Act I of 1894) was claimed as a matter of right under section 53 arid 54 of the said Act. Section 53 provides that the provisions of Civil Procedure Code shall apply to all proceedings before the Court under the Act so far as they are not inconsistent with anything contained in the Act. Section 54 as it stood at that time did not contain any provision for an appeal to His Majesty in Council, but provided for an appeal to the High Court subject to the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code applicable to appeals from the original decree. It was, however, contended before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on behalf of the appellant in the above-mentioned case that though the right of appeal must be found in the statute under which the proceeding had been taken, but that, in view of section 53 of the Act, the Court on reference should be deemed to have made, after hearing, a 'decree' or 'order' from which an appeal lay under section 109 of the Civil Procedure Code. Lord Macnaghton who delivered the judgment of the Judicial Committee quoted with approval the following observation of Lord Bramwell as made in the judgment in the case of Sand Back Charity Trustees Vs. The North Stafford-shire Railway Co., reported in 1897 (3) Q.B. D.I. 

 26. Similar view was expressed by Lord Atkin in an appeal to the Judicial Committee from West Africa in the case of Cohence Moore Vs. Akessch Payee, reported in AIR 1935 PC 5 in the following statement :— 

 27. A Division Bench of the Dacca High Court was confronted with a similar question when they were called upon to decide in the case or Hari Meah Vs. State, reported in 10 DLR 123 whether there was a right of appeal against an order of conviction and sentence made by Special Magistrate under the provisions of section 6 of the East Pakistan Food (Special Courts) Act, (E.P. Act X of 1956). In the said Act there was no specific provision for appeal but section 8 of the Act provided that the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure in so far as they were applicable and were not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act might apply to all matters connected with, arising from or consequent upon a trial by Special Magistrate appointed under the said Act. It was held in the said case that the Special Magistrate under the said Act was not a Magistrate under the Code of Criminal Procedure and as such was not a Criminal Court within the meaning of the Code so as to make his order appealable under the said Code without any provision in that behalf in the statute constituting him a criminal court. Hamoodur Rahman, J (as he then was) who delivered the judgment of the Bench stated the law in the following words: 

 28. The view of the Dacca High Court as expressed in the above-mentioned case was approved by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Hari Meah Vs. The State, reported in 11 D.L.R. (S.C) 368 same case P.L.D. 1959 S.C. (Pak) 307. 

 30. We may examine here another pro-position which was stated by Viscount Haldane L.C. in the case of National Telephone Company Limited Vs. His Majesty's Post Master General, reported in (1913) A.C. 546 (H.L.) in the following way: 

 31. It may be urged that the proceeding for assessment of compensation having been taken to the court in reference under the Land Acquisition Act all the incidents of a proceeding under the said. Act will attach to the said proceeding for assessment of compensation and that the ultimate order of assessment which may be made in the said proceeding will partake of the nature of the final order of assessment passed by the Court under the Land Acquisition Act and will be subject to appeal in the same manner as has been provided in the said Act. Reference may be made in this context to some decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, where a view has been taken that notwithstanding absence of an express provision for appeal, a decision made by a Court on appeal from an order passed by a non-judicial body becomes amenable to appeal because of the nature of the proceeding taken and the character of the decision making body. 

 32. In the case of the Secretary of State for India Vs. Chelikani Rama Rao, reported in L.R. 43 I.A. 192 same case I.L.R. 39 Mad. 617 same case 20 C.W.N. 1311, a question was raised as to the competency of a second appeal to the High Court against an appellate order made by the District Court pronouncing a decision against an order of Forest Settlement Officer under the provision of Madras Forest Act (Act V of 1882). It was argued in the said case relying upon the decision in the case of Rangoon Botatoung Company Ltd. Vs. The Collector, Rangoon L.R. 39 LA. 197 same case I.R.R. 40 Cal. 21 P.C. which we have considered above that no appeal lay from the order of the District Court, as there was no express provision for such an appeal in the Madras Forest Act. Lord Shaw in delivering the judgment on behalf of the Judicial Committee pointed out the distinction from the principle laid down in the Rangoon Botatoung Company Ltd's case and stated the law in the following terms at pages 197-198 of the report : 

 "In their Lordships' opinion, this objection is not well-founded. Their view is that when proceedings of this character reach the District Court, that court appealed to is one of the ordinary courts of the country, with regard to whose procedure, orders and decrees the ordinary rules of the Civil Procedure Code apply It was urged that the case of Rangoon Botatoung Company Vs. The Collector, Rangoon enounced a principle which formed a precedent for excluding all appeals from the decision of the District Court in such cases as the present. Their Lordships do not think that is so. In the Rangoon case a certain award had been made by the Collector under the Land Acquisition Act. This award was affirmed by the Court, which under the Act meant a principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction. Two judges sat as 'the Court' and also as the High Court to which appeal is given from the award of 'the Court'. The proceedings were, however, from beginning to end ostensibly and actually arbitration proceedings. In view of the nature of the question to be tried and the provisions of the particular statute, it was held that there was no right 'to carry an award made in an arbitration as to the value of land further than to the Court specifically set up by the statute for the determination of that value. The merits of the present dispute are essentially different in character. The claim was the assertion of a legal right to possession of and property in land; and if the ordinary courts of the country are seized of a dispute of that character, it would require, in the opinion of the Board, a special limitation to exclude the ordinary incidents of litigation. The objection taken is accordingly repelled." 

 33. The Judicial Committee has clearly explained that the proceeding before the Court in reference under the Land Acquisition Act for determination of the value of the land is essentially an arbitration proceeding and that the character of the tribunal being that of an arbitrator, in spite of its being the principal civil court of the District, the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code are not necessarily attracted for the purpose of making the order a judicial one and thus, amenable to appeal according to the Code. 

 36. The Judicial Committee reiterated this view in the case of R.M.A.R.A. Adaikappa Chettiar and another Vs. R. Chandrasekhare Thever, L.R. 74 I.A. 264 same case 52 C.W.N. 275 same case 1948 P.C. 12 and Lord Simons, delivering the judgment of the Judicial Committee, made the following statement of law : 

 37. As we have seen, the Court deciding a dispute as to assessment of compensation under the Land Acquisition Act does not function as an ordinary court of the country but as an arbitrator, and therefore the ordinary rules of procedure as contained in the Code of Civil Procedure are not attracted in respect of such a proceeding for assessment of compensation nor is the order passed by such a court a judicial order, except is in so far as it is other-directed in the statute under which such a court acts. 

 38. It should, however, be noticed that a dispute may arise in a proceeding under the Land Acquisition Act as to the title of a claimant to the compensation money and in such a case there may be a reference to the Land Acquisition Court for the determination of such a question. Such kind of proceeding may be distinguished from the one which is merely concerned with the assessment of compensation money to be determined on the basis of the value of the land. The Judicial Committee of Privy Council clearly brought out the distinction between the two kinds of proceeding taken under the Land Acquisition Act in the case of T.B. Rama Chandra Rao Vs. A.N.S. Rama Chandra Das, reported in L.R. 49 LA 129 same case 26 C.W.N. 713 same case A.I.R. 1922 P.C. 80 while explaining the principle laid down in the earlier case of The Rangoon Botatoung Company Ltd. Vs. The Collector, Rangoon and Lord Buekmaster in delivering the judgment of the Judicial Committee in the said case made the following observation at pages 136-137 of the report after referring to the decision in the Rangoon case: 

 "There appears to be some misapprehension in the Courts in India as to the effect of this authority which it is desirable should be removed. Under the Land Acquisition Act there are two perfectly separate and distinct fern s of procedure contemplated. The first is that is necessary for fixing the amount of the compensation and this is being described as an award. By section 54, an appeal from that award or any part of the award is given to the High Court. The case in Rangoon Botatoung Company Limited, L.R. 39 I.A. 197 decided that in those circumstances the appeal so given was the only one open to the parties, and that even if appealed against, the award still retained its characteristics and was incapable of further appeal. The argument which succeeded in that case emphasises the distinction between an award and a decree, and the judgment mentions this in terms by stating that the Appellant, although admitted to the High Court could not have the right to carry an award made under an arbitration as to the value of land taken for public purposes up to this Board as if it were a decree of the High Court made in course of its original jurisdiction. The manifest inconvenience that would attend any such proceeding is also pointed out, but neither this judgment nor any other judgment of this Board affects the question of an appeal on the totally different proceedings that arise when there is a dispute as between the persons claiming compensation involving, as it does in this case, a different question of title when Once the award as to the amount has become final, all questions as to fixing of compensation are then at an end ; the duty of the Collector in case of dispute as to the relative right of the persons together entitled to the money is to place money under the control of the Court and the parties can proceed to litigate in the ordinary way to determine what their right and title to the property may be." 

 39. In the said case which arose out of a suit for declaration as to the title of a person who earlier obtained a judgment from the High Court on an appeal from a decision as to such title in a proceeding under the Land Acquisition Act, it was held that the said judgment would be res judicata in the subsequent suit on the following reasons, as stated at page 137 of the report : 

 "The award as constituted by statute is nothing but an award which states the area of the land, the compensation to be allowed and the apportionment among the persons interested in the land of whose claim the Collector has information, meaning thereby people whose interests are not in dispute, but from the moment when the sum has been deposited in Court under section 31(2), the functions of the award have ceased ; and all that is left is a dispute between interested people as to the extent of their interest. Such dispute forms no part of the award, and it would indeed be strange if a controversy between two people as to the nature of their respective interests in a piece of land should enjoy certain right of appeal which would be wholly taken away when the piece of land was represented by a sum of money paid into Court. There has in the present case been a clear decision upon the very point now in dispute which cannot be reopened." 

 41. As we have noticed above, according to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, a Land Acquisition Court making assessment of compensation on the basis of the value of the land acts as an arbitrator and the proceeding for assessment of compensation is a kind of arbitration proceeding, but when such a court determines any question pertaining to the title of the parties in respect of the compensation assessed in a proceeding under the Land Acquisition Act, it functions as a Court of law and the proceeding is in the nature of a judicial proceeding. In a case which is concerned only with the assessment of compensation, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure will therefore he no guide for determining whether the assessment made by the Court is subject to further scrutiny by a superior Court. 

 42. It has been contended on behalf of the appellant that the land Acquisition Act and the Town Improvement Act are statutes in pari materia and as such both of them should be regarded as one system and complementary to each other. It is no doubt true that the rule laid down with respect to the Acts in pari materia, in what is known as Palmer's case Rex Vs. Palmer (1785 ) I Leach C.C. 4th Ed. (355 ) which has been accepted by the Judicial Authorities in England as a useful canon, is that such Acts "are to be taken together as forming one system and as interpreting and enforcing each other", but that does not mean that the provision of one Act which does not apply in terms in respect of the matters dealt with in the other Act should be made applicable in respect of the said matters merely on the ground that the said Acts are in pari materia. The true meaning of the said rule is that the words or expressions used in an earlier state which have been statutorily defined or judicially interpreted are generally presumed to bear the same meaning in the later Act as in the said statutory definition or judicial interpretation. It is permissible to call in aid the meaning given to the words in an earlier Act i in pari materia for the purpose of interpreting same words in the later Act used in similar connection. As has been held in the case of Lenhon Vs. Gibson and Howes Ltd., reported in 1919 A.C. 709, where the Legislature has given to words statutory definition in one statute and have used the same words in a similar connection in a later statute dealing with the same subject matter, it may be presumed, in the absence of any context indicating contrary intention, that the same meaning attaches to the words in the later statute as given to them in the earlier statute. But there appears to be no authority for the contention, as has been urged by the learned Attorney-General, that the provision of an earlier statute in pari materia which is not applicable in terms in respect of the-subject matter of the later statute can be made use of for the purpose of enlarging or limiting the scope of the provisions of the later statute. 

 43. The law on the subject as is understood in England, has been stated in the Halsbury's Laws of England, 3rd Edition, Vol 36 page 402 to the following effect: 

 44. The Land Acquisition Act of 1894 is a statute which contains provisions for compulsory acquisition of lands for public purpose and for companies, and for assessment of compensation in respect of such lands. The Town Improvement Act of 1953 was enacted for the purpose of development, improvement and expansion of the towns of Dacca and Narayanganj along with the lands in the vicinity, and Chapter IV of the said Act comprising sections 79 to 93 embodies provisions for compulsory acquisition of land and assessment of compensation for the lands acquired for the purposes of the said Act. Section 79 of the Act lays down that Government may acquire land for the aforesaid purposes under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act of 1894 and under section 80 a Tribunal is to be constituted for the purpose of performing the functions of the Court in reference under the Land Acquisition Act viz. compulsory acquisition of land and determination of compensation in respect of such land. Section 81 provides for modification of certain provisions of the Land Acquisition Act for the purpose of acquisition of land for the Board and according to the said section an award of the Tribunal shall be deemed to be an award of the Court under the Land Acquisition Act and, subject to the provisions of section 88 which provides for appeal under certain circumstances, shall be final. Under section 87(2) every award of the Tribunal shall be enforced by the Civil Court of competent jurisdiction as if it were a decree of that court. 

 45. By the amending Ordinance of 1958 (East Pakistan Ordinance No. LXIX of 1958) section 93A was inserted in the Town Improvement Act providing for special procedural rules for the purpose of acquisition of lands for the Board. It may be noted that neither the Land Acquisition Act nor the Town Improvement Act, as originally enacted, did contain any provisions for requisition of land. For the purpose of taking over lands under section 93A which may be required by the Board for carrying out the purposes of the Act, the proceeding starts with requisition of the land so required under subsection (1) and possession is taken under sub-section (3). Under the amending Ordinance of 1958, the requisitioning authority was the Provincial Government, but by a further amendment effected by East Pakistan. Ordinance No. VI of 1963, the power of requisition has been conferred on the Deputy Com-missioner who on being directed by the Government may exercise the said power. If the Govt. thinks fit to acquire the requisitioned property, steps are taken under clauses (a) to (i) of sub-section (4) of section 93A for acquisition of the said land. Clauses (a) and (b)(i) of sub-section (5) of the said section lay down procedure for the determination of compensation by agreement and., in default of any agreement, by the Deputy Commissioner. Under sub-clause (ii) clause (b) of sub-section (5) any party interested who has not accepted the assessment made by the Deputy Commissioner may move the Tribunal to determine the matter i.e., assessment of compensation, Sub-clause (iii) of clause (b) as well as clause (c) of the said sub-section lay down the procedure for determination of the assessment by the Tribunal. Sub-section (6) enacts that when any property is requisitioned or acquired under section 93A provisions of section 88 and 91 which provide for appeal against certain decisions of the Tribunal shall not apply. 

 46. There is no dispute as to the finality of the assessment of compensation made by the Tribunal under the provision of section 93A but the controversy which has been sought to be raised is as to the finality of such assessment made by the Court functioning under the Land Acquisition Act by virtue of section 91A of the Town Improvement Act in the absence of the Tribunal. It is to be examined whether, because of failure of the Government to constitute a Tribunal, a basis change occurs as to the nature of the proceeding or the character of the assessment-making body so as to make its assessment appealable in spite of the positive provision to the contrary in the general provision of section 93A. 

 "If the Provincial Government does not constitute a Tribunal in accordance with the provisions of section 80, all references to the Tribunal in section 64, 93A and 95 and sub-section (1) of Section 96 and in the schedule of this Act shall be construed as referring to the Court under the Land Acquisition Act of 1894". 

 49. Under the general provisions of the Town Improvement Act a Tribunal is to be constituted under section 80 of the Act for the purpose of performing the functions of the Court in reference to the acquisition of the land for the Board under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act. These functions are mainly concerned with the determination of assessment of compensation in case the interested parties refuse to accept the assessment made by the Deputy Commissioner. By virtue of the provision of section 91A which is now in force the Land Acquisition Court, namely, the Principal Civil Court of the District is to perform the said functions in the absence of a Tribunal constituted under the Town Improvement Act. It has already been mentioned that for the purpose of assessment of compensation in respect of the and acquired for the purpose of the Town Improvement Act, all the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act have not been made applicable. The schedule to the Town Improvement Act, as has been referred to in section 81 of the Act, has enumerated the modifications of the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act for their applicability for the purpose of acquisition of lands under the Town Improvement Act. 

 50. We have already noticed that section 93A which was introduced by amending ordinance of 1958 and was subsequently amended by E.P. Ordinance No. VI of 1963, lays down an entirely different procedure for acquisition of land for the purpose of Town Improvement Act and for assessment of compensation for such land. Ordinarily it is the Tribunal which shall have to perform such functions under the said provisions and the determination of compensation of assessment there under is not open to appeal in view of the barring provision contained in sub-section (6). In default of the constitution of a Tribunal the Provincial Government was to appoint under the old 'section 91A a Judge of the High Court or District Judge as an Arbitrator for determining the assessment of compensation in case any interested party did not accept the assessment made under sub-clause (i) of clause (b) of sub-section (5) of section 93A. The old section 91A contemplated ad-hoc appointment of an Arbitrator in each particular case. This position was brought to an end by the new section 91A as introduced in 1963 which provides a kind of permanent appointment of an Arbitrator in the shape of the Land Acquisition. Court in the absence of a duly constituted Tribunal. 

 51. As we have seen, if the Tribunal made a determination of assessment under section 93A, such determination was not open to appeal in view of sub-section (6) of the said section. If an ad-hoc Arbitrator appointed under the old section 91A, who had to be a judge of the High Court or a District Judge made such a determination that also was not open to appeal in view of sub-section (3) of the said section 91A. In the new section 91A introduced in 1963 which has been drafted in a different language; there is no express provision like sub-section (3) of the old section of 91A barring appeal from the award given by the ad-hoc Arbitrator. The question is whether in view of the fact that an assessment made by the Land Acquisition Court under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act is subject to appeal under section 54 of the Act and that there is no barring provision as to appeal in the new section 91A, the determination of assessment made by such a Court under the provisions of section 93A is amendable to appeal. We shall have to be clear in our mind that the determination of a disputed assessment made by the Land Acquisition Court by virtue of Section 91A is made under section 93A of the Town Improvement Act and not under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act. Section 93A has no doubt made certain provisions of the Land Acquisition Act applicable for the purpose of assessment made under the said section, as indicated in clause (b)(i) of sub-section (5) of Section 93A but it has nowhere been provided that the determination made by the said Court under section 93A shall be deemed to be an award of the said Court within the meaning of section 26 or section 54 of the Land Acquisition Act. It is pertinent to refer to the important rule of construction of statutes which is to be followed in a case where certain provisions of a different statute are incorporated in another statute by reference. The rule has been stated in the Halsbury's Laws of England 3rd Edition Vol. 36 at page 404 paragraph 611 which may be quoted as follows: 

 53. We shall have to bear in our mind another well-known maxim as an aid to interpretation of statutes viz. Expressio unius est exclusio alterius that is, express mention of one thing or person implies the exclusion of other things or persons. Where certain specific provisions of a statute have been expressly mentioned or referred in another statute, for the purpose of the latter, the legislative intent appears to be that the provisions which have not been so declared or referred have been deliberately excluded. It is no doubt true that some caution is to be exercised in applying this maxim to construe a statute, as there may have been an inclusion of certain thing or person for the purpose of abundant caution, or an exclusion on account of some inadvertance or accident in drafting the statute. But if there were in fact such inclusion or exclusion, the application of the maxim in such a case would lead to a kind of inconsistency or injustice which will belie such a legislative in-tent. In this case, there seems to be no indication of such inconsistency or injustice. The position therefore appears to be clear that the provisions of section 26 or 54 of the Land Acquisition Act having not been mentioned along with the other sections of the Lard Acquisition Act, which have been made applicable for the purpose of determination of assessment made under section 93A, it may be naturally concluded that exclusion of the said provisions was the legislative intent. 

 54. We may, however, be induced to accept the contrary view if the terms of section 26 or 54 themselves on true interpretation compel its to accede to such a view. 'The provisions of section 26 and section 54 of the Land Acquisition Act may be usefully quoted for the proper appreciation of the matter. The provisions are to the following effect: 

 "26(1) Every award under this Part shall be in writing signed by the Judge, and shall specify the amount awarded under clause first of sub-section (1) of section 23, and also the amounts if any respectively awarded under each of the other clauses of the same sub-section, together with the grounds of awarding each of the said amounts. (2) Every such award shall be deemed to be a decree and the statement of the grounds of every such award a judgment within the meaning of section 2, clause (2), and section 2, clause (9) respectively; of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (V of 1908)". 

 55. As we see, section 26, as quoted above, provides that "every award, under this Part" i.e., Part III of the Land Acquisition Act shall be drawn up in certain from and every such award shall be deemed to be decree and the grounds of such an award a judgment. The determination of assessment under section 93A, sub-section (5)(b)(ii) cannot be said to be an award made under Part III of the Land Acquisition Act. The provisions of Part III consisting Sections 18 to 28 comprise special provisions to be followed by the Court in reference for the determination of the objection to the award made by the Collector under the said Act. These provisions are not at all attracted for the determination of a similar question under section 93A. Of these Sections, only sections 23 and 24, which have been substantially modified by the schedule to the Town Improvement Act, are applicable. By the said schedule another new section, namely, Section 24A which has been inserted in the Land Acquisition Act by the said schedule has also been made applicable. In these circumstances it can hardly be said that the determination made under section 93A of the Town Improvement Act can be regarded as an award under Part III of the Land Acquisition Act. Similarly section 54 of the Land Acquisition Act also has no application, as the assessment in question made under section 93A is not an award within the meaning of the Land Acquisition Act nor can it be said to be made in a proceeding under the Land Acquisition Act. 

 56. The intent of the Legislature appears to be clear from the provisions of sub-section (6) of section 93A which provides that when any property is requisitioned or acquired under the said section the provisions of sections 88 and 91 shall not apply. Section 88 is the only provision under the Town Improvement Act which provides for an appeal against a decision of the Tribunal under Certain circumstances. The only change which. the Legislature' has directed in respect of section 93A, in the event of non-constitution of a Tribunal by the Government, is the substitution of the Court functioning under the Land Acquisition Act in place of the Tribunal in sub-clause (ii) of sub-section (5)(b) under which any person interested who has not accepted the assessment may move for determination of the assessment of compensation and in clause (e) of sub-section (5) under which the parties concerned shall have to state their respective cases in respect of a fair amount of compensation at the commencement of the proceeding. Sub-section (6) which excludes the provision of appeal as contained in the Town Improvement Act is not altered in any way. The Legislative intent seems to be clear on a perusal of the entire provisions of section 93A that the determination of assessment made under the said Section after any property has been requisitioned or acquired shall be final. It does not appear to be in consonance with good reason that the Legislature wanted that there would be no appeal if the Government constituted a Tribunal but if the Government did not constitute the Tribunal the assessment should be opened to in appeal to the High Court and a further appeal to the Supreme Court. The intention seems to be clear that if land is acquired under the provisions of Section 93A this assessment is not open to appeal. 

 58. On the question of the exercise of the revisional jurisdiction by the High Court, it may be pointed out that I have already held that a Land Acquisition Court in assessing compensation on the basis of the value of the land acquired does not function as an ordinary. Court and the proceedings before it for determination of such compensation, as has been explained by the Judicial Committee in the cases of the Secretary of State for India Vs. Chelikani Rama. Rao L.R. 43 I.A. 192 and Hem Singh Vs. Basant Das L.R. 63 I.A. 180 are "from beginning to end ostensibly and actually arbitration proceedings" and not judicial proceedings in a Court of law which are amenable to further scrutiny by a Superior Court under the Code. I am therefore of opinion that the High Court was wrong in exercising its powers under Section 115 of the Cede with respect to the order of assessment made under Section 93A of the Town Improvement Act and its order setting aside the direction of the Land Acquisition Court as to payment of interest is liable to set aside. 

 The result is that this appeal is dismissed with costs and the order of the High Court dismissing the appeal preferred to it is maintained, but its order rescinding the direction of the Land Acquisition Court as to payment of interest is set aside.
